To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the microlensing optical depth is a sensitive function of the axis ratio of a self-consistent bar, and (2) the mass of the microlenses is a sensitive function both of the axis ratio and the velocity distribution of a self-consisting bar.
the microlensing mass is a factor of 5 more uncertain than the simple Poisson uncertainty and the typical microlens mass is about a factor of two higher in Freeman bars compared to other models.

the microlensing rate is proportional to the bar length and the bar velocity dispersion, but inversely proportional to the square of the bar axis ratio and to the square of its angle to the line of sight.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of microlensing in the inner Galaxy, in particular the Galactic bar.
the following questions: (i) What is the mass of the lens? (ii) How do the lens mass, axis ratio and bar velocity distribution depend on each other?
the study of the dynamics of the inner Galaxy using the data on the microlensing rate.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the microlensing rate is consistent with a typical lens mass in the range 0.2–0.8 M _{⊙}, depending on the model used.
the microlensing rate towards the Galactic bulge depends on the bar model in the following order: Freeman bar > Miyamoto-Nagai bar > Sawa-Noguchi bar.
the microlensing data are consistent with a typical lens mass around 0.3 M⊙, but that the mass is not well constrained.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
microlensing data alone are not sufficient for determining the lens mass, and that a combination of kinematic data and microlensing data will be required to break the non-uniquenous degeneracy.

, for the same microlensing event rates, Freeman bar models imply a lens mass of about 0.8 M⊙, whereas the models with a bar angle closer to the line of sight and with a more isotropic velocity distribution (such as those by Binney et al. or Zhao & Evans) imply a typical lens masses of 0.2 M⊙.
the lens mass is not yet well constrained by microlensing observations.
The main takeaway from our work is that
microlensing observations can be a very sensitive probe of the dynamics of the bar.
the microlensing rate is sensitive to the details of the bar model, which in turn is sensitive to the kinematic data available.
the microlensing rate towards the bulge is not only a probe of the stellar density distribution, but also a probe of the kinematics of the bar.
